policy: Review every closed candidate set. Select only when ASV wording or an explicit mapped textual note distinguishes a reading; otherwise mark underdetermined and retain the base fallback. The base candidate is the SBLGNT reading.

decisions.evidence: ASV 'And when he had agreed' renders either an initial kai or a postpositive de as 'And'; the participle stands first in English regardless of Greek order, so nothing in the verse distinguishes the readings.
ASV 'Again he went out' carries no connective, but ASV leaves a linking de untranslated often enough that its absence does not exclude the added particle; neither reading is distinguished.

ASV 'about the eleventh hour' supplies 'hour' as the idiomatic English for a bare feminine ordinal of time (cf. 'about the sixth and the ninth hour', v.5), so the word does not show whether hōran stood in the Greek.
ASV has 'found others standing' with no qualifier, and renders 'idle' only in the following question ('Why stand ye here all the day idle?'). The added argous after hestōtas is unrepresented.
ASV ends the verse at 'Go ye also into the vineyard'; the added clause 'and whatsoever is right, that shall ye receive' has no counterpart in the English.
ASV 'pay them their hire' renders an explicit indirect object 'them' alongside the accusative 'hire'; the omission would leave only 'pay the hire'.
ASV 'And when they came' renders either kai with the participle or a postpositive de as 'And'; the English is identical under both readings.
ASV 'And when the first came' renders either kai elthontes or elthontes de as 'And when ... came'; nothing distinguishes them.
pleion and pleiona are alternate accusative forms of the same comparative; ASV 'more' renders either.
The readings differ only in Greek word order and the presence of the article to; ASV 'and they likewise received every man a shilling' fixes its own English order and shows neither.
The added hoti after legontes is recitative, introducing direct speech; ASV renders it with the comma and quotation of 'saying, These last...', so its presence or absence leaves no trace.
The readings differ only in the order of the pronouns; English grammar fixes 'made them equal unto us' either way.
The readings differ only in whether the verb precedes or follows 'to one of them'; ASV 'said to one of them' is the required English order under both.

ASV begins the verse 'Is it not lawful for me' with no disjunctive, while it does render the later ē of this same verse as 'or is thine eye evil'; the translators represent ē where they read it, so the added initial Ē is absent.
The readings differ only in whether the infinitive precedes or follows the relative clause; ASV 'to do what I will' is the same English under both.
ASV 'or is thine eye evil, because I am good?' renders a disjunctive ē; the variant Ei ('if') would give a conditional, which the English interrogative does not.
ASV ends the verse at 'and the first last'; the added clause 'for many are called, but few chosen' is wholly unrepresented.

ASV 'And as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem' renders a present participle of ascent with 'Jesus' as subject; the variant's mellōn ('being about to go up') would require 'was about to go up', which the ASV does not have.
ASV reads 'the twelve disciples', an explicit noun that the omission of mathētas ('the twelve') would leave unsupported.

ASV 'apart, and on the way he said unto them' renders both the conjunction and the phrase 'on the way', which excludes the reading that drops en tē hodō (r02). Between the remaining two only the position of kai differs, and the English conjunction placement does not settle it.
ASV 'he shall be raised up' is passive, matching egerthēsetai; ASV consistently renders anistēmi in this formula as 'rise again', which it does not do here.
par' and ap' with the genitive after 'asking' are both rendered by English 'of him'; ASV 'asking a certain thing of him' shows neither preposition.
ASV renders an explicit second-person possessive at every point in the request — 'thy right hand', 'thy left hand', 'thy kingdom' — leaving no slot where sou is unrepresented.
ASV asks only 'Are ye able to drink the cup that I am about to drink?'; the added baptism clause 'or to be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with' is absent.

ASV opens the verse 'He saith unto them' with no conjunction; ASV regularly renders a clause-initial kai as 'And' (so 'And he said', 'And behold' through this chapter), so the added Kai is not in view.
ASV reads 'My cup indeed ye shall drink: but to sit...'; the added clause 'and with the baptism that I am baptized withal shall ye be baptized' has no counterpart.

ASV 'on my right hand, and on my left hand' supplies 'hand' for both substantival adjectives, and English idiom repeats the possessive with the repeated noun; the second 'my' is therefore not evidence that mou stood after euōnymōn.
ASV 'is not mine to give' has no demonstrative; the added touto would be rendered 'this is not mine to give'.

ASV 'Not so shall it be among you' is future, which excludes the present estin (r02). Between the two future readings only the connective de differs, and ASV supplies no 'but' or 'and' here while freely omitting a linking de elsewhere, so it is not settled.
an and ean are interchangeable in this indefinite relative construction; ASV 'whosoever would become great' renders either.
an and ean are interchangeable in this indefinite relative construction; ASV 'whosoever would be first' renders either.
ASV 'shall be your servant' is a future indicative, matching estai; the imperative estō would be rendered 'let him be your servant'.

ASV 'saying, Lord, have mercy on us' places the vocative before the imperative, which excludes the transposed reading Eleēson hēmas kyrie (r02). The two remaining readings differ only in the printed comma, which English punctuation requires in any case.
ASV 'thou son of David' is direct address, which renders the nominative-for-vocative huios and the vocative huie alike.
ASV 'they cried out the more' does not mark aspect; the aorist ekraxan and imperfect ekrazon are both rendered so.

ASV 'saying, Lord, have mercy on us' places the vocative first, excluding the transposed Eleēson hēmas kyrie (r02); the remaining two differ only in the printed comma, which the English punctuates the same way regardless.
ASV 'thou son of David' is direct address and renders the nominative huios and the vocative huie identically.
The readings differ in the aorist passive form of anoigō and in word order; ASV 'that our eyes may be opened' renders both alike.
ommatōn and ophthalmōn are both rendered 'eyes'; ASV 'touched their eyes' shows no distinction.
ASV 'straightway they received their sight' makes the men the subject of the verb; the added autōn hoi ophthalmoi would give 'their eyes received sight', with 'eyes' as subject.
